opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the great missed opportunities in Canadian health care, honestly. And I say that as someone who works in Ontario and sees the consequences of it pretty much every day in my research.

When you look at what Ontario has in principle, it should be one of the best places in the world to do health data science. We have a single-payer system, a large and incredibly diverse population, and decades of administrative data. But the clinical data, the really rich stuff that lives in the electronic medical records, is fragmented across hospitals, across vendors, across primary care practices. One hospital might be on one system, the hospital down the street on another, and the family doctor on something else entirely. They often don't talk to each other.

From a patient's perspective, that means you end up repeating your history over and over, tests get duplicated, and important information falls through the cracks during transitions of care. From a research and AI perspective, it means that a huge amount of effort goes into just cleaning, harmonizing, and linking data before you can ask a single meaningful question. I'd estimate the majority of the time on many of our projects is spent on that plumbing rather than the science.

I don't think it failed because people didn't see the value. There were real investments, and some of them were well-intentioned but poorly executed. Part of it is governance. Health care in Ontario is delivered by many semi-independent organizations, each making its own procurement decisions. Part of it is the privacy landscape, which is important, but which has sometimes been interpreted in a way that makes institutions very risk-averse about sharing. And part of it is simply that nobody was given the mandate and the sustained funding to say, "this is the standard, and everyone is going to adopt it."

What gives me some hope is that there's now a much clearer understanding of why this matters, particularly with machine learning. You can't build reliable, generalizable models if your data is siloed and inconsistent. So I'd love to see us move toward common data standards and federated approaches, where the data doesn't necessarily all have to live in one place but can be queried and analyzed in a consistent, privacy-preserving way. We don't necessarily need one monolithic system. We need interoperability, and we need the political will to make it happen.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think "failure" is the right word, but it's a failure of coordination rather than of technology or even of intent. Ontario has spent, by some counts, billions of dollars over two decades trying to get there, and what we ended up with is a patchwork. Every hospital network, every family health team, every lab and imaging centre essentially chose its own vendor and its own standards, and nobody had the authority or the political will to force them onto one system.

From where I sit, doing medical imaging and AI research, the cost of that is very concrete. If I want to build a model that predicts how a cancer patient will respond to treatment, I need the imaging, the pathology, the bloodwork, the medication history, and the outcomes, all linked to the same person over time. In Ontario, those live in four or five different systems that don't talk to each other, with different patient identifiers and different consent regimes. So an enormous amount of the work isn't science, it's plumbing. Cleaning, matching, negotiating data-sharing agreements hospital by hospital.

And the thing that frustrates me is that we're a single-payer system. Every one of those patients is funded by the same province. In principle this should be easier here than almost anywhere in the world. Alberta, interestingly, has done more with Netcare and now Connect Care, and you can see the difference in what researchers there can do.

I'd also say the harm isn't only to research. Patients are the ones carrying paper records between appointments, repeating tests, having drug interactions missed. The AI conversation sometimes makes it sound like the data problem is abstract, but it starts with whether your family doctor can see what the emergency department did last week.

So my view is that it's a solvable problem, and it's mostly a governance problem. You need a mandated standard, a single identifier, and someone accountable for making it happen. Until then, we'll keep building clever workarounds for a system that shouldn't need them.

astra-6.text: I see it as a missed opportunity. When medical records don’t connect across institutions, it’s harder for clinicians to get a complete picture of a patient’s care, and patients end up having to fill in the gaps themselves. A common system could also help us learn from the data and improve care, but it has to be built around privacy, public trust, and the needs of patients and clinicians.
